ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, three satellites a, b, and c of the same mass move in uniform circular motion around the Earth, among which b and c are on the Earth's synchronous orbit, and a is at a height R from the Earth's surface. At this moment a and b are exactly at their closest distance. It is known that the Earth's mass is M, its radius is R, the angular velocity of the Earth's rotation is ω, and the universal gravitational constant is G, then (　　)
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: Satellite a and b still need to pass $\mathrm{t=}\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{8\mathrm{R}^{3}}}-\omega}$ before they are next at their closest distance

At this moment a and b are exactly at their closest distance. ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: Satellite a and b still need to pass $\mathrm{t=}\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{8\mathrm{R}^{3}}}-\omega}$ before they are next at their closest distance
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the Earth is located at the center, satellite a is on the relatively inner dashed circular orbit, and satellites b and c are on the relatively outer dashed circular orbit; currently a and b are located on the same straight-line direction on the right side of the Earth's center, with a inside and b outside, so the angle between the two relative to the Earth's center is 0, and the figure also shows that they are arranged along the same radial direction at this moment. The inner and outer orbits in the figure both have arrows of motion in the same direction. Reasoning: When the orbital radii of two satellites doing circular motion are fixed, their distance satisfies d^2 = r_a^2 + r_b^2 - 2r_a r_b cosθ, where θ is the angle between the two relative to the Earth's center; when θ=0, the distance is minimum. Initially the angle between a and b is 0, so for the next closest distance, a is required to turn one more circle relative to b, that is, the relative angular displacement is 2π. According to the meaning of the problem, the Earth's radius is R, and a is at a height R from the Earth's surface, so a's orbital radius r_a = R + R = 2R. For a, use universal gravitation to provide centripetal force: GMm/(2R)^2 = m(2R)Ω_a^2, simplifying gives Ω_a^2 = GM/(8R^3), so Ω_a = √(GM/(8R^3)). b is on the Earth's synchronous orbit, so its angular velocity Ω_b = ω. From the figure showing the outer orbit outside the inner orbit, it can be known that a's angular velocity is greater than that of synchronous satellite b, therefore the next closest distance satisfies (Ω_a - Ω_b)t = 2π, namely (√(GM/(8R^3)) - ω)t = 2π. Solving gives t = 2π/(√(GM/(8R^3)) - ω).
